blocks.text: K. stared at the Inspector. Was he receiving schoolmasterly lessons here from a man perhaps younger than himself? Was he being punished with a reprimand for his frankness? And of the reason for his arrest and the one who had ordered it, was he to learn nothing?

He fell into a certain agitation, walked up and down, which no one prevented him from doing, pushed back his cuffs, felt his chest, smoothed his hair, passed by the three gentlemen, said, “It is quite senseless,” whereupon they turned toward him and looked at him obligingly, yet seriously, and finally came to a halt again before the Inspector's table. “The Public Prosecutor Hasterer is my good friend,” he said, “may I telephone him?” “Certainly,” said the Inspector, “but I do not know what sense that could have, unless it should be that you have some private affair to discuss with him.” “What sense?” cried K., more dismayed than annoyed. “Who are you, then? You demand sense and put on the most senseless performance there is. Is it not enough to soften a stone? First these gentlemen fell upon me, and now they sit or stand around here and make me go through my paces before you. What sense it would have to telephone a Public Prosecutor when I am supposedly under arrest? Very well, I shall not telephone.” “Oh, but do,” said the Inspector, stretching out his hand toward the anteroom where the telephone was, “please do telephone.” “No, I no longer wish to,” said K., and went to the window. Across the way the company was still at the window and seemed only now, because K. had stepped up to the window, to be slightly disturbed in the calm of their watching. The old people were about to rise, but the man behind them calmed them. “There are more such spectators over there,” K. called out quite loudly to the Inspector, pointing outside with his forefinger. “Away from there,” he then shouted across. The three did indeed retreat a few steps at once, the two old people even behind the man, who shielded them with his broad body and, to judge by the movements of his mouth, said something unintelligible at that distance. They did not vanish entirely, however, but seemed to be waiting for the moment when they could approach the window again unnoticed. “Intrusive, inconsiderate people!” said K., as he turned back into the room. The Inspector possibly agreed with him, as K. thought he could tell from a sidelong glance. Yet it was just as possible that he had not been listening at all, for he had pressed one hand firmly onto the table and seemed to be comparing the lengths of his fingers. The two warders sat on a trunk draped with an ornamental cloth and rubbed their knees. The three young men had placed their hands on their hips and looked aimlessly about. It was as quiet as in some forgotten office. “Well, gentlemen,” cried K., it seemed to him for a moment as though he were carrying them all upon his shoulders, “to judge by your appearance, my affair would seem to be concluded. I am of the opinion that it is best to reflect no further on the justification or lack of justification of your proceedings and to bring the matter to a conciliatory close by a mutual handshake. If you too are of my opinion, then please”—and he stepped up to the Inspector's table and held out his hand to him. The Inspector raised his eyes, chewed his lips, and looked at K.'s outstretched hand; K. still believed the Inspector would clasp it. He, however, stood up, took a hard round hat that was lying on Fräulein Bürstner's bed, and placed it carefully on his head with both hands, as one does when trying on new hats. “How simple everything seems to you!” he said to K. as he did so; “we should bring the matter to a conciliatory close, you thought? No, no, that really will not do. By which, on the other hand, I by no means wish to say that you should despair. No, why indeed? You are merely under arrest, nothing more. That was what I had to inform you of, I have done so, and I have also seen how you have taken it. With that, it is enough for today and we can take our leave, though only provisionally. You will no doubt wish to go to the bank now?” “To the bank?” asked K., “I thought I was under arrest.” K. asked with a certain defiance, for although his handshake had not been accepted, he felt himself, especially since the Inspector had stood up, ever more independent of all these people. He was playing with them. He intended, should they leave, to run after them as far as the street door and offer them his arrest. Therefore he also repeated: “How can I possibly go to the bank, since I am under arrest?” “Oh, I see,” said the Inspector, who was already at the door, “you have misunderstood me. You are under arrest, certainly, but that is not to hinder you from carrying out your profession. Nor are you to be hindered in your ordinary way of life.” “Then being under arrest is not very bad,” said K., and walked close up to the Inspector. “I never meant it otherwise,” said the latter. “It seems, however, that even the notification of the arrest was not very necessary then,” said K., and stepped closer still. The others too had drawn nearer. All of them were now gathered in a narrow space by the door. “It was my duty,” said the Inspector. “A stupid duty,” said K. unyieldingly. “May be,” replied the Inspector, “but let us not waste our time with such talk. I had assumed that you wished to go to the bank. Since you pay close attention to every word, I will add: I am not forcing you to go to the bank, I had only assumed that you wished to. And to make that easier for you, and to render your arrival at the bank as inconspicuous as possible, I have kept these three gentlemen, your colleagues, here at your disposal.” “What?” cried K., and stared in astonishment at the three. These so featureless, anemic young men, whom he still remembered only as a group by the photographs, were indeed clerks from his bank—not colleagues, that was saying too much and already a gap in the Inspector's omniscience, yet subordinate clerks from the bank they certainly were. How could K. have overlooked that? How absorbed he must have been by the Inspector and the warders not to have recognized these three. Stiff Rabensteiner, swinging his hands, fair-haired Kullich with his deep-set eyes, and Kaminer with the insufferable smile caused by a chronic muscular twitch—“Good morning!” said K. after a little while and offered his hand to the gentlemen, who bowed correctly. “I did not recognize you at all. Well then, we shall go to work, shall we not?” The gentlemen nodded, laughing and eager, as though they had been waiting for this the entire time; only when K. missed his hat, which had been left behind in his room, did they all run one after another to fetch it, which after all suggested a certain embarrassment. K. stood still and watched them go through the two open doors; the last was naturally the indifferent Rabensteiner, who had merely broken into an elegant trot. Kaminer handed over the hat, and K. had to tell himself expressly, as was moreover often necessary at the bank as well, that Kaminer's smile was not intentional, indeed that he could not smile intentionally at all. In the anteroom Frau Grubach, who did not look very guilt-ridden at all, then opened the apartment door for the whole company, and K. looked down, as he so often did, at her apron string, which cut so unnecessarily deep into her massive body. Downstairs K., watch in hand, decided to take an automobile, so as not to increase unnecessarily a delay that was already half an hour long. Kaminer ran to the corner to fetch the car, while the other two obviously tried to distract K., when suddenly Kullich pointed to the street door opposite, in which the tall man with the blond pointed beard was just appearing and, in the first instant a little embarrassed at showing himself now at his full height, stepped back to the wall and leaned against it. The old people were probably still on the stairs. K. was annoyed with Kullich for drawing attention to the man whom he himself had already seen earlier, whom indeed he had even been expecting. “Do not look over there,” he burst out, without noticing how striking such a manner of speaking was toward independent men. No explanation was necessary, however, for just then the automobile arrived, they got in, and drove off. Then K. recalled that he had not noticed the departure of the Inspector and the warders at all; the Inspector had obscured the three clerks from him, and now in turn the clerks had obscured the Inspector. That did not demonstrate much presence of mind, and K. resolved to observe himself more closely in this respect. Still, he turned around involuntarily and leaned forward over the back of the automobile, in order, if possible, still to see the Inspector and the warders. Yet at once he turned back again and leaned comfortably into the corner of the car without having even made the attempt to look for anyone. Although it did not appear so, he would have needed encouragement just now, but the gentlemen now seemed fatigued; Rabensteiner looked out of the car to the right, Kullich to the left, and only Kaminer was at his disposal with his grin, about which humanity unfortunately forbade making a jest.
